title: Pair Employees with Their Direct Managers
description_markdown: Perform a SELF JOIN on `employees` to find each employee's direct manager. Return `e.first_name AS employee_name` and `m.first_name AS manager_name`. Order by `e.emp_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join employees e and employees m
SELECT e.first_name AS employee_name, m.first_name AS manager_name
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON ...
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee_name, m.first_name AS manager_name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Self-joining aliases the table twice: `e` as employee and `m` as manager on `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
hints: Join condition: `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
Focus on the required WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY clause conditions.
Query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee_name, m.first_name AS manager_name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC;

title: Find Employees Who Earn More Than Their Manager
description_markdown: Find all employees whose salary is strictly higher than their manager's salary. Return `e.first_name AS employee`, `e.salary AS emp_salary`, `m.first_name AS manager`, and `m.salary AS mgr_salary`. Order by `e.emp_id`.
starter_query:
-- Self-join comparing salaries
SELECT ...
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee, e.salary AS emp_salary, m.first_name AS manager, m.salary AS mgr_salary FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Compares compensation between connected subordinate and supervisor records.
hints: Join on `e.manager_id = m.emp_id` and filter with `WHERE e.salary > m.salary`.
Focus on the required WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY clause conditions.

Query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee, e.salary AS emp_salary, m.first_name AS manager, m.salary AS mgr_salary FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC;

title: Generate Matrix of Categories and Target Countries
description_markdown: Generate all possible pairs of category names from `categories` and distinct customer countries from `customers` using a CROSS JOIN. Return `c.category_name` and `u.country`. Order by `c.category_name` ASC, `u.country` ASC.
starter_query:
-- CROSS JOIN categories and distinct countries
SELECT ...
solution_query: SELECT c.category_name, u.country FROM categories c CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers) u ORDER BY c.category_name ASC, u.country ASC;
solution_explanation: A CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product matching every left row with every right row.
hints: Use `CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers) u`.
Focus on the required WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY clause conditions.
Query: SELECT c.category_name, u.country FROM categories c CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers) u ORDER BY c.category_name ASC, u.country ASC;

title: Find Coworker Pairs Reporting to the Same Manager
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to find distinct pairs of coworkers who report to the same manager (`e1.manager_id = e2.manager_id`). Use `e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id` to eliminate reflexive self-pairs and duplicates. Return `e1.first_name AS emp_1`, `e2.first_name AS emp_2`, and `e1.manager_id`. Order by `manager_id` ascending, `emp_1` ascending, `emp_2` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join to find coworker peers
SELECT e1.first_name AS emp_1, e2.first_name AS emp_2, e1.manager_id
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e1.first_name AS emp_1, e2.first_name AS emp_2, e1.manager_id FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id = e2.manager_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id ORDER BY e1.manager_id ASC, emp_1 ASC, emp_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Self-joining with condition `e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id` pairs distinct coworkers sharing a supervisor without mirroring results (A-B and B-A).
common_mistakes: Using `!=` instead of `<` which causes inverted duplicate rows.
interview_tip: To generate unique undirected pairs in SQL, always use `<` on the primary key.
hints: Join on `e1.manager_id = e2.manager_id`.
Filter with `AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id`.

Query: SELECT e1.first_name AS emp_1, e2.first_name AS emp_2, e1.manager_id FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id = e2.manager_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id ORDER BY e1.manager_id ASC, emp_1 ASC, emp_2 ASC;

title: Map Subcategories to Parent Categories
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `categories` to map each subcategory to its parent category on `sub.parent_category_id = parent.category_id`. Return `sub.category_name AS sub_category` and `parent.category_name AS parent_category`. Order by `parent_category` ascending, then `sub_category` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join on categories hierarchy
SELECT sub.category_name AS sub_category, parent.category_name AS parent_category
FROM categories sub
JOIN categories parent ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT sub.category_name AS sub_category, parent.category_name AS parent_category FROM categories sub JOIN categories parent ON sub.parent_category_id = parent.category_id ORDER BY parent_category ASC, sub_category ASC;
solution_explanation: Resolves the adjacency list hierarchy by self-joining on `parent_category_id = category_id`.
common_mistakes: Reversing the parent and child alias logic.
interview_tip: Adjacency lists are the simplest way to store trees in relational databases; traversing 1 level is a simple self-join.
hints: Join on `sub.parent_category_id = parent.category_id`.
Order by `parent_category ASC, sub_category ASC`.

Query: SELECT sub.category_name AS sub_category, parent.category_name AS parent_category FROM categories sub JOIN categories parent ON sub.parent_category_id = parent.category_id ORDER BY parent_category ASC, sub_category ASC;

title: Find Pairs of Classmates in the Same Major
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `students` to pair students enrolled in the same major (`s1.major = s2.major`). Filter with `s1.student_id < s2.student_id`. Return `s1.first_name AS student_1`, `s2.first_name AS student_2`, and `s1.major`. Order by `s1.major` ascending, `student_1` ascending, `student_2` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join on major
SELECT s1.first_name AS student_1, s2.first_name AS student_2, s1.major
FROM students s1
JOIN students s2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT s1.first_name AS student_1, s2.first_name AS student_2, s1.major FROM students s1 JOIN students s2 ON s1.major = s2.major AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id ORDER BY s1.major ASC, student_1 ASC, student_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Forms cohort classmate pairings by matching equal majors while deduplicating pairs via student ID inequality.
common_mistakes: Omitting student_id < student_id, leading to self-matching (Alice with Alice).
interview_tip: Self-matches occur whenever an equality join is performed on the same table without primary key exclusion.
hints: Join on `s1.major = s2.major`.
Filter `AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id`.

Query: SELECT s1.first_name AS student_1, s2.first_name AS student_2, s1.major FROM students s1 JOIN students s2 ON s1.major = s2.major AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id ORDER BY s1.major ASC, student_1 ASC, student_2 ASC;

title: Pair Employees Working in the Same Department
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to pair staff working in the same department (`e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id`). Restrict to `e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id`. Return `e1.first_name AS emp_1`, `e2.first_name AS emp_2`, and `e1.dept_id`. Order by `e1.dept_id` ascending, `emp_1` ascending, `emp_2` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join on dept_id
SELECT e1.first_name AS emp_1, e2.first_name AS emp_2, e1.dept_id
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e1.first_name AS emp_1, e2.first_name AS emp_2, e1.dept_id FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id ORDER BY e1.dept_id ASC, emp_1 ASC, emp_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Matches departmental colleagues without pairing employees with themselves or generating duplicate permutations.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the table alias qualifier in the SELECT list.
interview_tip: Always verify whether the interviewer wants ordered pairs (permutations) or unordered pairs (combinations with `<`).
hints: Join on `e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id`.
Order by `e1.dept_id ASC, emp_1 ASC, emp_2 ASC`.

Query: SELECT e1.first_name AS emp_1, e2.first_name AS emp_2, e1.dept_id FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id ORDER BY e1.dept_id ASC, emp_1 ASC, emp_2 ASC;

title: Find Coworkers with Identical Compensation
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to find distinct pairs of employees earning the exact same salary (`e1.salary = e2.salary`). Use `e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id`. Return `e1.first_name AS emp_1`, `e2.first_name AS emp_2`, and `e1.salary`. Order by `e1.salary` descending, `emp_1` ascending, `emp_2` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join on salary match
SELECT e1.first_name AS emp_1, e2.first_name AS emp_2, e1.salary
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e1.first_name AS emp_1, e2.first_name AS emp_2, e1.salary FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.salary = e2.salary AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id ORDER BY e1.salary DESC, emp_1 ASC, emp_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Surfaces pay parity matches across the company roster.
common_mistakes: Sorting salary ascending instead of descending.
interview_tip: Self-joins are ideal for identifying value ties or duplicates without needing an aggregate GROUP BY.
hints: Join on `e1.salary = e2.salary AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id`.
Order by `e1.salary DESC, emp_1 ASC, emp_2 ASC`.

Query: SELECT e1.first_name AS emp_1, e2.first_name AS emp_2, e1.salary FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.salary = e2.salary AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id ORDER BY e1.salary DESC, emp_1 ASC, emp_2 ASC;

title: Find Pairs of Customers Residing in the Same City
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `customers` to find pairs residing in the same city (`c1.city = c2.city`). Filter with `c1.customer_id < c2.customer_id`. Return `c1.first_name AS cust_1`, `c2.first_name AS cust_2`, and `c1.city`. Order by `c1.city` ascending, `cust_1` ascending, `cust_2` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join on city
SELECT c1.first_name AS cust_1, c2.first_name AS cust_2, c1.city
FROM customers c1
JOIN customers c2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c1.first_name AS cust_1, c2.first_name AS cust_2, c1.city FROM customers c1 JOIN customers c2 ON c1.city = c2.city AND c1.customer_id < c2.customer_id ORDER BY c1.city ASC, cust_1 ASC, cust_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Groups distinct customer neighbors who live in the same geographic municipality.
common_mistakes: Matching customers against themselves.
interview_tip: Always enforce primary key inequality to prevent self-matches.
hints: Join on `c1.city = c2.city AND c1.customer_id < c2.customer_id`.
Order by `c1.city ASC, cust_1 ASC, cust_2 ASC`.

Query: SELECT c1.first_name AS cust_1, c2.first_name AS cust_2, c1.city FROM customers c1 JOIN customers c2 ON c1.city = c2.city AND c1.customer_id < c2.customer_id ORDER BY c1.city ASC, cust_1 ASC, cust_2 ASC;

title: Generate Matrix of Departments and Distinct Job Titles
description_markdown: Generate all potential staffing roles per department by performing a `CROSS JOIN` between `departments` and the distinct `job_title` values from `employees`. Return `d.dept_name` and `jobs.job_title`. Order by `d.dept_name` ascending, then `jobs.job_title` ascending.
starter_query:
-- CROSS JOIN departments and distinct job titles
SELECT d.dept_name, jobs.job_title
FROM departments d
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT job_title FROM employees) jobs
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, jobs.job_title FROM departments d CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT job_title FROM employees) jobs ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, jobs.job_title ASC;
solution_explanation: CROSS JOIN creates the Cartesian product between every active department and every unique corporate job designation.
common_mistakes: Crossing the raw employees table instead of the distinct derived subquery, causing duplicate job title rows.
interview_tip: CROSS JOINs with distinct subqueries are commonly used in data modeling to generate full reporting grids.
hints: Use `CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT job_title FROM employees) jobs`.
Order by `d.dept_name ASC, jobs.job_title ASC`.
Query: SELECT d.dept_name, jobs.job_title FROM departments d CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT job_title FROM employees) jobs ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, jobs.job_title ASC;

title: Generate Matrix of Order Statuses and Payment Methods
description_markdown: Generate all possible combinations of order statuses and payment methods by performing a `CROSS JOIN` between distinct `order_status` from `orders` and distinct `payment_method` from `payments`. Return `os.order_status` and `pm.payment_method`. Order by `os.order_status` ascending, then `pm.payment_method` ascending.
starter_query:
-- CROSS JOIN distinct statuses and methods
SELECT os.order_status, pm.payment_method
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT order_status FROM orders) os
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT payment_method FROM payments) pm
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT os.order_status, pm.payment_method FROM (SELECT DISTINCT order_status FROM orders) os CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT payment_method FROM payments) pm ORDER BY os.order_status ASC, pm.payment_method ASC;
solution_explanation: Forms the complete Cartesian matrix across operational order lifecycle states and transaction gateways.
common_mistakes: Leaving off DISTINCT in the derived tables.
interview_tip: Cartesian grids are essential when building data cubes or checking for sparse data combinations.
hints: Wrap distinct selections in subqueries before cross joining.
Order by `os.order_status ASC, pm.payment_method ASC`.

Query: SELECT os.order_status, pm.payment_method FROM (SELECT DISTINCT order_status FROM orders) os CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT payment_method FROM payments) pm ORDER BY os.order_status ASC, pm.payment_method ASC;

title: Generate Academic Matrix of Majors and Active Semesters
description_markdown: Perform a `CROSS JOIN` between distinct `major` values from `students` and distinct `semester` values from `enrollments`. Return `m.major` and `s.semester`. Order by `m.major` ascending, then `s.semester` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Cross join distinct majors and semesters
SELECT m.major, s.semester
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT major FROM students) m
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT semester FROM enrollments) s
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT m.major, s.semester FROM (SELECT DISTINCT major FROM students) m CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT semester FROM enrollments) s ORDER BY m.major ASC, s.semester ASC;
solution_explanation: Produces all theoretical major and semester pairings for academic curriculum planning.
common_mistakes: Crossing tables directly without deduping.
interview_tip: A Cartesian product of N rows and M rows produces exactly N * M rows.
hints: Cross join two derived distinct tables.
Order by `m.major ASC, s.semester ASC`.
Query: SELECT m.major, s.semester FROM (SELECT DISTINCT major FROM students) m CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT semester FROM enrollments) s ORDER BY m.major ASC, s.semester ASC;

title: Identify Staff Hired Before Their Manager
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to find employees whose `hire_date` is strictly earlier than their manager's `hire_date`. Return `e.first_name AS employee_name`, `e.hire_date AS emp_hire_date`, `m.first_name AS manager_name`, and `m.hire_date AS mgr_hire_date`. Order by `e.emp_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Find employees hired before manager
SELECT e.first_name AS employee_name, e.hire_date AS emp_hire_date, m.first_name AS manager_name, m.hire_date AS mgr_hire_date
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee_name, e.hire_date AS emp_hire_date, m.first_name AS manager_name, m.hire_date AS mgr_hire_date FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id WHERE e.hire_date < m.hire_date ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Finds tenured team members who pre-date their current direct supervisor at the firm.
common_mistakes: Confusing the manager and employee hire dates.
interview_tip: This is a frequent SQL interview question testing hierarchical self-joins combined with temporal comparisons.
hints: Join condition: `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
Filter condition: `WHERE e.hire_date < m.hire_date`.

Query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee_name, e.hire_date AS emp_hire_date, m.first_name AS manager_name, m.hire_date AS mgr_hire_date FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id WHERE e.hire_date < m.hire_date ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC;

title: Count Direct Reports per Manager Using Self Join
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to count direct subordinates per manager (`e.manager_id = m.emp_id`). Group by `m.emp_id` and `m.first_name`. Return `m.first_name AS manager_name` and `COUNT(e.emp_id) AS direct_reports_count`. Order by `direct_reports_count` descending, then `manager_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join and count direct reports
SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS direct_reports_count
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS direct_reports_count FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name ORDER BY direct_reports_count DESC, manager_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Counts subordinate employees linked to each supervisor ID in the employee table.
common_mistakes: Grouping by e.emp_id instead of m.emp_id.
interview_tip: Remember that the manager record is m, and the subordinate record is e.
hints: Join condition: `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
Group by `m.emp_id, m.first_name`.

Query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS direct_reports_count FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name ORDER BY direct_reports_count DESC, manager_name ASC;

title: Filter Managers with at Least 3 Direct Reports
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to identify managers with at least 3 direct reports. Group by `m.emp_id` and `m.first_name`. Filter with `HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) >= 3`. Return `m.first_name AS manager_name` and `COUNT(e.emp_id) AS direct_reports_count`. Order by `direct_reports_count` descending, then `manager_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join with HAVING threshold
SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS direct_reports_count
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON ...
GROUP BY ...
HAVING ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS direct_reports_count FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) >= 3 ORDER BY direct_reports_count DESC, manager_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Filters managers by team size using aggregate HAVING on the self-join.
common_mistakes: Placing the count filter in WHERE.
interview_tip: Combining self-joins with HAVING is an intermediate-level query pattern favored by engineering interviewers.
hints: Join on `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
Filter with `HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) >= 3`.

Query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS direct_reports_count FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) >= 3 ORDER BY direct_reports_count DESC, manager_name ASC;

title: Calculate Total Subordinate Payroll per Manager
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to compute the total salary earned by each manager's direct reports. Group by `m.emp_id` and `m.first_name`. Return `m.first_name AS manager_name` and `SUM(e.salary) AS team_payroll`. Order by `team_payroll` descending, then `manager_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Calculate team payroll per manager
SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, SUM(e.salary) AS team_payroll
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, SUM(e.salary) AS team_payroll FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name ORDER BY team_payroll DESC, manager_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Sums subordinate salaries per supervisor record.
common_mistakes: Summing the manager's own salary instead of the subordinates'.
interview_tip: Ensure e.salary is summed rather than m.salary.
hints: Join condition: `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
Use `SUM(e.salary) AS team_payroll`.

Query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, SUM(e.salary) AS team_payroll FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name ORDER BY team_payroll DESC, manager_name ASC;

title: Calculate Average Subordinate Compensation per Manager
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to compute the average compensation of direct subordinates per manager. Group by `m.emp_id` and `m.first_name`. Return `m.first_name AS manager_name` and `ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_team_salary`. Order by `avg_team_salary` descending, then `manager_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Average team salary per manager
SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_team_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_team_salary FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name ORDER BY avg_team_salary DESC, manager_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Computes the mean direct subordinate salary per manager.
common_mistakes: Rounding without two decimal places.
interview_tip: Reporting metrics per manager helps HR monitor team compensation equity.
hints: Join on `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
Use `ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_team_salary`.

Query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_team_salary FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name ORDER BY avg_team_salary DESC, manager_name ASC;

title: Find Students with Identical GPA in Different Majors
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `students` to identify pairs of students who have the exact same GPA (`s1.gpa = s2.gpa`) but belong to different majors (`s1.major != s2.major`). Enforce `s1.student_id < s2.student_id`. Return `s1.first_name AS student_1`, `s1.major AS major_1`, `s2.first_name AS student_2`, `s2.major AS major_2`, and `s1.gpa`. Order by `s1.gpa` descending, `student_1` ascending, `student_2` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Self join matching GPA across different majors
SELECT s1.first_name AS student_1, s1.major AS major_1, s2.first_name AS student_2, s2.major AS major_2, s1.gpa
FROM students s1
JOIN students s2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT s1.first_name AS student_1, s1.major AS major_1, s2.first_name AS student_2, s2.major AS major_2, s1.gpa FROM students s1 JOIN students s2 ON s1.gpa = s2.gpa AND s1.major != s2.major AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id ORDER BY s1.gpa DESC, student_1 ASC, student_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Compares academic achievement metrics across distinct collegiate departments.
common_mistakes: Omitting s1.student_id < s2.student_id.
interview_tip: Combining equality on one column and inequality on another in a self-join is a powerful analytical query pattern.
hints: Conditions: `s1.gpa = s2.gpa AND s1.major != s2.major AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id`.
Order by `s1.gpa DESC, student_1 ASC, student_2 ASC`.

Query: SELECT s1.first_name AS student_1, s1.major AS major_1, s2.first_name AS student_2, s2.major AS major_2, s1.gpa FROM students s1 JOIN students s2 ON s1.gpa = s2.gpa AND s1.major != s2.major AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id ORDER BY s1.gpa DESC, student_1 ASC, student_2 ASC;

title: Find Similar Category Products with Price Spread Under 50
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `products` to find product pairs in the same category (`p1.category_id = p2.category_id`) where `p1.product_id < p2.product_id` and the absolute price difference `ABS(p1.price - p2.price) <= 50.00`. Return `p1.product_name AS product_1`, `p1.price AS price_1`, `p2.product_name AS product_2`, `p2.price AS price_2`, and `ROUND(ABS(p1.price - p2.price), 2) AS price_diff`. Order by `price_diff` ASC, `product_1` ASC, `product_2` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Self join on products with close prices
SELECT p1.product_name AS product_1, p1.price AS price_1, p2.product_name AS product_2, p2.price AS price_2, ROUND(ABS(p1.price - p2.price), 2) AS price_diff
FROM products p1
JOIN products p2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p1.product_name AS product_1, p1.price AS price_1, p2.product_name AS product_2, p2.price AS price_2, ROUND(ABS(p1.price - p2.price), 2) AS price_diff FROM products p1 JOIN products p2 ON p1.category_id = p2.category_id AND p1.product_id < p2.product_id WHERE ABS(p1.price - p2.price) <= 50.00 ORDER BY price_diff ASC, product_1 ASC, product_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Identifies competitive substitute goods in the same product category with closely matched pricing.
common_mistakes: Forgetting ABS() which would cause negative difference logic errors.
interview_tip: ABS(a - b) <= threshold is the standard method for finding proximate values in numerical columns.
hints: Join on `p1.category_id = p2.category_id AND p1.product_id < p2.product_id`.
Filter with `WHERE ABS(p1.price - p2.price) <= 50.00`.

Query: SELECT p1.product_name AS product_1, p1.price AS price_1, p2.product_name AS product_2, p2.price AS price_2, ROUND(ABS(p1.price - p2.price), 2) AS price_diff FROM products p1 JOIN products p2 ON p1.category_id = p2.category_id AND p1.product_id < p2.product_id WHERE ABS(p1.price - p2.price) <= 50.00 ORDER BY price_diff ASC, product_1 ASC, product_2 ASC;

title: Find Orders Placed on the Same Date by Different Customers
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `orders` to find pairs of orders placed on the exact same date (`o1.order_date = o2.order_date`) by different customers (`o1.customer_id != o2.customer_id`). Use `o1.order_id < o2.order_id`. Return `o1.order_id AS order_1`, `o1.customer_id AS cust_1`, `o2.order_id AS order_2`, `o2.customer_id AS cust_2`, and `o1.order_date`. Order by `o1.order_date` ASC, `order_1` ASC, `order_2` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Self join on order_date
SELECT o1.order_id AS order_1, o1.customer_id AS cust_1, o2.order_id AS order_2, o2.customer_id AS cust_2, o1.order_date
FROM orders o1
JOIN orders o2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT o1.order_id AS order_1, o1.customer_id AS cust_1, o2.order_id AS order_2, o2.customer_id AS cust_2, o1.order_date FROM orders o1 JOIN orders o2 ON o1.order_date = o2.order_date AND o1.customer_id != o2.customer_id AND o1.order_id < o2.order_id ORDER BY o1.order_date ASC, order_1 ASC, order_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Detects concurrent order activity from separate consumer accounts on a common calendar date.
common_mistakes: Allowing the same customer to match their own multiple orders on that date.
interview_tip: Filtering customer_id != customer_id isolates cross-customer behaviors.
hints: Join condition: `o1.order_date = o2.order_date AND o1.customer_id != o2.customer_id AND o1.order_id < o2.order_id`.
Order by `o1.order_date ASC, order_1 ASC, order_2 ASC`.

Query: SELECT o1.order_id AS order_1, o1.customer_id AS cust_1, o2.order_id AS order_2, o2.customer_id AS cust_2, o1.order_date FROM orders o1 JOIN orders o2 ON o1.order_date = o2.order_date AND o1.customer_id != o2.customer_id AND o1.order_id < o2.order_id ORDER BY o1.order_date ASC, order_1 ASC, order_2 ASC;

title: Traverse Two-Level Management Reporting Chains
description_markdown: Perform a double `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to trace employee `e`, their direct manager `m` (`e.manager_id = m.emp_id`), and their skip-level manager `sm` (`m.manager_id = sm.emp_id`). Return `e.first_name AS employee`, `m.first_name AS manager`, and `sm.first_name AS skip_manager`. Order by `e.emp_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Double self-join to traverse 2 tiers
SELECT e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager, sm.first_name AS skip_manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON ...
JOIN employees sm ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager, sm.first_name AS skip_manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id JOIN employees sm ON m.manager_id = sm.emp_id ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Chains two self-joins along the supervisor hierarchy to reveal two full tiers of managerial governance.
common_mistakes: Joining sm directly to e instead of m.
interview_tip: Before recursive CTEs were widely supported, self-joining multiple times was the standard pattern for fixed-depth tree traversal.
hints: Join `m` on `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
Join `sm` on `m.manager_id = sm.emp_id`.

Query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager, sm.first_name AS skip_manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id JOIN employees sm ON m.manager_id = sm.emp_id ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC;

title: Generate Marketing Targeting Matrix via CROSS JOIN
description_markdown: Perform a `CROSS JOIN` between `customers` and `products` where `c.country = 'USA'` and `p.price > 500`. Return `c.customer_id` and `p.product_id`. Order by `c.customer_id` ascending, then `p.product_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- CROSS JOIN filtered customers and products
SELECT c.customer_id, p.product_id
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN products p
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.customer_id, p.product_id FROM customers c CROSS JOIN products p WHERE c.country = 'USA' AND p.price > 500 ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC, p.product_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Constructs all prospective pairing candidates for premium marketing ad targeting in the US.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the country or price filter in the WHERE clause.
interview_tip: Filtering before or during cross-joins controls the Cartesian product size and prevents memory overflows.
hints: Use `FROM customers c CROSS JOIN products p`.
Filter `WHERE c.country = 'USA' AND p.price > 500`.
Query: SELECT c.customer_id, p.product_id FROM customers c CROSS JOIN products p WHERE c.country = 'USA' AND p.price > 500 ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC, p.product_id ASC;

title: Find Course Pairs Sharing Dept and Credit Count
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `courses` to find pairs of courses in the same department with the same credit count (`c1.department = c2.department AND c1.credits = c2.credits`). Restrict to `c1.course_id < c2.course_id`. Return `c1.course_code AS course_1`, `c2.course_code AS course_2`, `c1.department`, and `c1.credits`. Order by `c1.department` ASC, `course_1` ASC, `course_2` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Self join on courses department and credits
SELECT c1.course_code AS course_1, c2.course_code AS course_2, c1.department, c1.credits
FROM courses c1
JOIN courses c2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c1.course_code AS course_1, c2.course_code AS course_2, c1.department, c1.credits FROM courses c1 JOIN courses c2 ON c1.department = c2.department AND c1.credits = c2.credits AND c1.course_id < c2.course_id ORDER BY c1.department ASC, course_1 ASC, course_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Pairs curricular equivalents offering identical unit credits in the same academic field.
common_mistakes: Failing to enforce course_id inequality.
interview_tip: Multi-column joins with primary key inequality produce clean, non-redundant match lists.
hints: Join on `c1.department = c2.department AND c1.credits = c2.credits AND c1.course_id < c2.course_id`.
Order by `c1.department ASC, course_1 ASC, course_2 ASC`.

Query: SELECT c1.course_code AS course_1, c2.course_code AS course_2, c1.department, c1.credits FROM courses c1 JOIN courses c2 ON c1.department = c2.department AND c1.credits = c2.credits AND c1.course_id < c2.course_id ORDER BY c1.department ASC, course_1 ASC, course_2 ASC;

title: Pair Faculty Colleagues in the Same Department
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `professors` to find pairs of colleagues within the same department (`p1.department = p2.department`). Enforce `p1.professor_id < p2.professor_id`. Return `p1.last_name AS prof_1`, `p2.last_name AS prof_2`, and `p1.department`. Order by `p1.department` ASC, `prof_1` ASC, `prof_2` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Self join on professors department
SELECT p1.last_name AS prof_1, p2.last_name AS prof_2, p1.department
FROM professors p1
JOIN professors p2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p1.last_name AS prof_1, p2.last_name AS prof_2, p1.department FROM professors p1 JOIN professors p2 ON p1.department = p2.department AND p1.professor_id < p2.professor_id ORDER BY p1.department ASC, prof_1 ASC, prof_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Forms faculty peer committees within university departments.
common_mistakes: Using `!=` which returns duplicate reversed rows.
interview_tip: Using `<` ensures each pair is emitted exactly once in canonical alphabetical/numerical sequence.
hints: Join on `p1.department = p2.department AND p1.professor_id < p2.professor_id`.
Order by `p1.department ASC, prof_1 ASC, prof_2 ASC`.

Query: SELECT p1.last_name AS prof_1, p2.last_name AS prof_2, p1.department FROM professors p1 JOIN professors p2 ON p1.department = p2.department AND p1.professor_id < p2.professor_id ORDER BY p1.department ASC, prof_1 ASC, prof_2 ASC;

title: Calculate Consecutive Pay Raises via Self Join
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `salaries_history` to compare compensation records for the same employee where `sh1.emp_id = sh2.emp_id` and `sh1.effective_date < sh2.effective_date`. Return `sh1.emp_id`, `sh1.effective_date AS prior_date`, `sh1.salary AS prior_salary`, `sh2.effective_date AS new_date`, and `sh2.salary AS new_salary`. Order by `sh1.emp_id` ASC, `prior_date` ASC, `new_date` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Self join on salary history dates
SELECT sh1.emp_id, sh1.effective_date AS prior_date, sh1.salary AS prior_salary, sh2.effective_date AS new_date, sh2.salary AS new_salary
FROM salaries_history sh1
JOIN salaries_history sh2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT sh1.emp_id, sh1.effective_date AS prior_date, sh1.salary AS prior_salary, sh2.effective_date AS new_date, sh2.salary AS new_salary FROM salaries_history sh1 JOIN salaries_history sh2 ON sh1.emp_id = sh2.emp_id AND sh1.effective_date < sh2.effective_date ORDER BY sh1.emp_id ASC, prior_date ASC, new_date ASC;
solution_explanation: Tracks progression intervals across employee compensation history using temporal self-join.
common_mistakes: Joining without matching emp_id.
interview_tip: Temporal self-joins were standard before window functions (LAG/LEAD) were introduced, and remain a classic technical question.
hints: Join on `sh1.emp_id = sh2.emp_id AND sh1.effective_date < sh2.effective_date`.
Order by `sh1.emp_id ASC, prior_date ASC, new_date ASC`.

Query: SELECT sh1.emp_id, sh1.effective_date AS prior_date, sh1.salary AS prior_salary, sh2.effective_date AS new_date, sh2.salary AS new_salary FROM salaries_history sh1 JOIN salaries_history sh2 ON sh1.emp_id = sh2.emp_id AND sh1.effective_date < sh2.effective_date ORDER BY sh1.emp_id ASC, prior_date ASC, new_date ASC;

title: Calculate Compensation Gap Between Manager and Staff
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` (`e.manager_id = m.emp_id`) to calculate the compensation premium `(m.salary - e.salary) AS salary_difference`. Return `e.first_name AS employee`, `m.first_name AS manager`, and `(m.salary - e.salary) AS salary_difference`. Order by `salary_difference` DESC, `employee` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Manager vs subordinate salary spread
SELECT e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager, (m.salary - e.salary) AS salary_difference
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager, (m.salary - e.salary) AS salary_difference FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id ORDER BY salary_difference DESC, employee ASC;
solution_explanation: Quantifies the compensation differential between direct reports and their immediate team supervisors.
common_mistakes: Subtracting employee salary from manager salary in reverse order.
interview_tip: Self-joining hierarchical data allows arithmetic difference calculations across org chart tiers.
hints: Join on `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
Calculate `(m.salary - e.salary) AS salary_difference`.

Query: SELECT e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager, (m.salary - e.salary) AS salary_difference FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id ORDER BY salary_difference DESC, employee ASC;

title: Generate Theoretical Dept-Project Planning Matrix
description_markdown: Perform a `CROSS JOIN` between `departments` and `projects`. Return `d.dept_name` and `p.project_name`. Order by `d.dept_name` ascending, then `p.project_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Full cross join
SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name
FROM departments d
CROSS JOIN projects p
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name FROM departments d CROSS JOIN projects p ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Forms every possible permutation between business departments and ongoing technology projects.
common_mistakes: Adding an ON clause to a CROSS JOIN.
interview_tip: CROSS JOIN takes no ON clause in standard ANSI SQL.
hints: Use `FROM departments d CROSS JOIN projects p`.
Order by `d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC`.
Query: SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name FROM departments d CROSS JOIN projects p ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;

title: Pair Customers with Successive Registration Timestamps
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `customers` to pair each customer with subsequent registrants who registered later (`c1.created_at < c2.created_at`) from the same country (`c1.country = c2.country`). Return `c1.first_name AS cust_1`, `c1.created_at AS created_at_1`, `c2.first_name AS cust_2`, and `c2.created_at AS created_at_2`. Order by `c1.country` ASC, `created_at_1` ASC, `created_at_2` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Self join on country and chronological order
SELECT c1.first_name AS cust_1, c1.created_at AS created_at_1, c2.first_name AS cust_2, c2.created_at AS created_at_2
FROM customers c1
JOIN customers c2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c1.first_name AS cust_1, c1.created_at AS created_at_1, c2.first_name AS cust_2, c2.created_at AS created_at_2 FROM customers c1 JOIN customers c2 ON c1.country = c2.country AND c1.created_at < c2.created_at ORDER BY c1.country ASC, created_at_1 ASC, created_at_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Chronologically orders user registrations within the same regional territory.
common_mistakes: Omitting the country equality filter.
interview_tip: Temporal joins partition chronological streams by categorical dimensions like country.
hints: Join condition: `c1.country = c2.country AND c1.created_at < c2.created_at`.
Order by `c1.country ASC, created_at_1 ASC, created_at_2 ASC`.

Query: SELECT c1.first_name AS cust_1, c1.created_at AS created_at_1, c2.first_name AS cust_2, c2.created_at AS created_at_2 FROM customers c1 JOIN customers c2 ON c1.country = c2.country AND c1.created_at < c2.created_at ORDER BY c1.country ASC, created_at_1 ASC, created_at_2 ASC;

title: Find Manager Leading the Highest Headcount
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to find the single manager who oversees the greatest number of direct reports. Group by `m.emp_id` and `m.first_name`. Return `m.first_name AS manager_name` and `COUNT(e.emp_id) AS team_size`. Order by `team_size` descending, then `manager_name` ascending. Limit to 1 row.
starter_query:
-- Top manager by team size
SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS team_size
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...
LIMIT 1;
solution_query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS team_size FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name ORDER BY team_size DESC, manager_name ASC LIMIT 1;
solution_explanation: Identifies the supervisor with the widest span of control using self-join aggregation and top-1 ranking.
common_mistakes: Leaving out LIMIT 1.
interview_tip: ORDER BY ... DESC LIMIT 1 is the most efficient ANSI SQL pattern to fetch top-1 records.
hints: Join condition: `e.manager_id = m.emp_id`.
Order by `team_size DESC, manager_name ASC LIMIT 1`.

Query: SELECT m.first_name AS manager_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS team_size FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.first_name ORDER BY team_size DESC, manager_name ASC LIMIT 1;

title: Pair Classmates Matriculating in the Same Year
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `students` to pair students entering in the same `enrollment_year` (`s1.enrollment_year = s2.enrollment_year`) but in different majors (`s1.major != s2.major`). Restrict with `s1.student_id < s2.student_id`. Return `s1.first_name AS student_1`, `s2.first_name AS student_2`, and `s1.enrollment_year`. Order by `s1.enrollment_year` ASC, `student_1` ASC, `student_2` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Self join on cohort year and different major
SELECT s1.first_name AS student_1, s2.first_name AS student_2, s1.enrollment_year
FROM students s1
JOIN students s2 ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT s1.first_name AS student_1, s2.first_name AS student_2, s1.enrollment_year FROM students s1 JOIN students s2 ON s1.enrollment_year = s2.enrollment_year AND s1.major != s2.major AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id ORDER BY s1.enrollment_year ASC, student_1 ASC, student_2 ASC;
solution_explanation: Pairs interdisciplinary classmates from the same entering college cohort.
common_mistakes: Allowing students with identical majors into the result.
interview_tip: Carefully combine equality and inequality predicates to isolate cohort sub-segments.
hints: Join on `s1.enrollment_year = s2.enrollment_year AND s1.major != s2.major AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id`.
Order by `s1.enrollment_year ASC, student_1 ASC, student_2 ASC`.

Query: SELECT s1.first_name AS student_1, s2.first_name AS student_2, s1.enrollment_year FROM students s1 JOIN students s2 ON s1.enrollment_year = s2.enrollment_year AND s1.major != s2.major AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id ORDER BY s1.enrollment_year ASC, student_1 ASC, student_2 ASC;

title: Generate Evaluation Grid of Categories and Star Ratings
description_markdown: Perform a `CROSS JOIN` between `categories` and distinct `rating` values from `reviews`. Return `c.category_name` and `r.rating`. Order by `c.category_name` ascending, then `r.rating` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Cross join categories and distinct ratings
SELECT c.category_name, r.rating
FROM categories c
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT rating FROM reviews) r
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.category_name, r.rating FROM categories c CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT rating FROM reviews) r ORDER BY c.category_name ASC, r.rating ASC;
solution_explanation: Generates an exhaustive matrix of feedback scores per retail catalog department.
common_mistakes: Omitting DISTINCT from the rating subquery, causing duplicate rows.
interview_tip: Always distinct derived dimension tables when generating analytical scoring grids.
hints: Use `CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT rating FROM reviews) r`.
Order by `c.category_name ASC, r.rating ASC`.
Query: SELECT c.category_name, r.rating FROM categories c CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT rating FROM reviews) r ORDER BY c.category_name ASC, r.rating ASC;

title: Rank Departments by Volume of Coworker Combinations
description_markdown: Perform a `SELF JOIN` on `employees` to count the total number of distinct coworker pairs within each department (`e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id`). Group by `e1.dept_id`. Return `e1.dept_id` and `COUNT(*) AS coworker_pairs`. Order by `coworker_pairs` descending, then `dept_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Count coworker combinations per department
SELECT e1.dept_id, COUNT(*) AS coworker_pairs
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e1.dept_id, COUNT(*) AS coworker_pairs FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id GROUP BY e1.dept_id ORDER BY coworker_pairs DESC, dept_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Computes the combination count n*(n-1)/2 of unique coworker pairings per organizational unit.
common_mistakes: Using e1.emp_id != e2.emp_id which counts permutations n*(n-1) instead of combinations.
interview_tip: The formula n*(n-1)/2 is matched in SQL by self-joining on `<` rather than `!=`.
hints: Join on `e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id`.
Group by `e1.dept_id` and count rows with `COUNT(*)`.

Query: SELECT e1.dept_id, COUNT(*) AS coworker_pairs FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.dept_id = e2.dept_id AND e1.emp_id < e2.emp_id GROUP BY e1.dept_id ORDER BY coworker_pairs DESC, dept_id ASC;
